newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia gunmen queue to beat disarmament deadline.
newsitem.headline: Liberia gunmen queue to beat disarmament deadline.

text.p: Liberia's militiamen, who have held the shattered nation hostage during seven years of civil war, queued on Friday to beat a midnight disarmament deadline designed to clear the way for elections in May.
Long queues formed at the capital's disarmament centres with some people carrying guns freshly dug up from the beach.

Several thousand child soldiers have already demobilised but it looked doubtful that all fighters would hand in their weapons on time. With estimates of the number of fighters ranging up to 60,000, only about 17,000 had disarmed by Friday morning.
U.N. monitors said, however, they would remain at collection points into Saturday and West African peacekeepers said they would still accept arms volunteered after the deadline.

"If one brings a weapon willingly to (the) ECOMOG (peacekeeping force), we will be there to receive it even after the deadline," the chief of staff of the Nigerian-led force, General Abdul-One, told reporters on Friday. "If we have to go out to look for them that will be a different thing," he added.
The civil war has killed well over 150,000 people in the West African country founded by freed American slaves in 1847.

Liberia's neighbours brokered the peace accord last August. Signed in Nigeria's capital Abuja, it followed a dozen collapsed accords and a flare-up in the capital during which hundreds of people died in an orgy of looting and fighting in April and May.
West African leaders have threatened individual sanctions against anyone derailing the deal.
ECOMOG commander General Victor Malu has said fighters found with guns after the deadline will be treated as criminals.
"We have made a tremendous improvement both in the quantity and the quality weapons surrended," George Nagash, head of the U.N. Humanitarian Coordination Office (UN-HACO), said.
"Until we all meet with ECOMOG tomorrow and make a decision about what happens after tonight's deadline, all UN-HACO staff will remain at their present locations."

Over a dozen collection points are scattered round the country. In a bid to give a final push to the disarmament process, civic groups offered free plots of land to demobilising fighters. Rice and help with education were on offer from the United Nations or the peacekeepers.
U.N. monitors said on Thursday that 16,838 gunmen had disarmed since the exercise began in November -- including 3,564 child soldiers and 1,046 women fighters.
Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war, and Alhadji Kromah, his sometime rival but his ally against ethnic Krahn factions in April and May, say they plan to run for president.
Their Krahn rival Roosevelt Johnson has said he plans to go into business rather than politics. All have pledged to disarm.
The war pitted the descendants of the slaves, grouped with indigenous allies within Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia, against the Krahn who supplanted them in the 1980s and their allies.

Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi said this week that West African peace monitors and faction leaders were reviewing the figure of 60,000 fighters -- given at the height of the war when warlords tended to exaggerate the size of their forces.
"We are working on a revised number between 20,000 and 60,000 but we think the realistic figure will be between 35,000 to 40,000 fighters that we expect to be disarmed," he added.
